stories.headline: Three CRPF men injured in Kulgam terror attack
stories.title: Three CRPF men injured in Kulgam terror attack
stories.summary: Attackers open fire on naka party, flee from spot Joint security operation launched CCTV footage scanned to identify attackers One critically injured jawan shifted to 92 Base Hospital, Srinagar Alert sounded across Kashmir as forces launch frisking operations Srinagar, Nov 11: Terrorists opened fire on a Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) checkpoint at Nowpora, Akhran near Mir Bazar in Kulgam district of south Kashmir on Wednesday, leaving three personnel injured, one of them critical. The attack took place around 2.15 pm when the assailants approached the checkpoint and fired several rounds at the CRPF party before fleeing from the spot. The targeted personnel belonged to the CRPF's 46th Battalion. The sudden gunfire triggered panic in the area, prompting security forces to rush reinforcements to the spot. The injured personnel were identified as Head Constable Somveer, Constables Santano and Rakesh Das. They sustained bullet injuries and were immediately shifted to the hospital for treatment. A CRPF official said that the injured were initially taken to Government Medical College (GMC), Anantnag. “One of the critically injured personnel was subsequently shifted to the 92 Base Hospital in Srinagar for advanced treatment, while the other two were reported to be stable,” he said. A police official told Rising Kashmir that after the attack, a massive manhunt has been launched in the area. Soon after the attack, Army, CRPF and Jammu and Kashmir Police personnel launched a joint search operation in the area. Security forces cordoned off the locality and intensified surveillance to track down the attackers. Investigators are also examining CCTV footage from the surrounding areas, including shops and other establishments, to establish the route taken by the assailants and identify their movements before and after the attack. The location is considered strategically important as Akhran and Mir Bazar lie close to the Jammu-Srinagar National Highway, a crucial road link connecting Kashmir with the rest of the country. A senior CRPF official said that the operations were underway to apprehend the perpetrators and assured that the injured personnel would receive the best possible medical treatment. The attack has renewed security concerns in south Kashmir, particularly amid continuing efforts by security agencies to dismantle terrorist networks and prevent attacks on security personnel and civilians. Investigators are now working to establish the identity of the attackers, their possible support network and the circumstances that enabled them to escape after targeting the CRPF checkpoint. There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack. Pertinently, Inspector General of Police (IGP) Kashmir Sujit Kumar recently told reporters that a local terrorist, along with foreign terrorists, was orchestrating attacks in south Kashmir. Meanwhile, security forces have sounded an alert across Kashmir, with frisking and search operations being intensified across Srinagar and other locations. Witnesses said that in various parts of Srinagar, including Lal Chowk, frisking operations were carried out post-attack.

stories.headline: The shared scars of the himalayan belt
stories.title: The shared scars of the himalayan belt
stories.summary: Nepal- The air above the Langtang Lirung peaks, high above 5,000 metres, has been warming quietly for decades, softening the ancient permafrost that binds rock to ice. On August 26, 2026, the mountain finally surrendered to the heat. What followed was not a mere landslide, but a 142-million-cubic-metre avalanche of bedrock, ice, and mud. The high-altitude collapse unleashed a violent flow that tore down the Lhende Khola, Bhote Koshi, and Trishuli river valleys at speeds exceeding 188 kilometres per hour. When the wall of debris slammed into the valley floor, the impact registered on seismographs as a 5.5-magnitude earthquake. In the lower valleys, there was no time to run. Within minutes, the infrastructure of modern Nepal was erased. The Gyirong border post vanished, concrete bridges shattered, and a violent surge overwhelmed vital hydropower plants, sealing hundreds of laborers deep within underground tunnels. Today, the silence in the Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts is broken only by the shifting mud and the desperate efforts of rescue teams. The human toll is baffling: at least 1,400 lives are confirmed lost, while families hold onto fading hope for more than 5,500 people still missing. Search operations have become an agonizing, dangerous gamble, fought across choked communication lines and mountains of debris. For scientists, tracing the source of the disaster took little time. A rapid attribution study conducted by the World Weather Attribution (WWA) research group pointed squarely at the invisible culprit: decades of global carbon emissions and human influence on the climate. The warming atmosphere has systematically destabilized the world’s highest peaks, turning frozen monuments into fluid hazards. The tragedy has left Nepal facing an estimated $4.8 billion (€4.2 billion) economic loss; an impossible figure for a nation already stumbling from consecutive years of unprecedented seasonal flooding. The crisis has forced Prime Minister Balendra Shah onto the international stage, transforming local mourning into a fierce diplomatic battle for international climate justice. Pushing the “polluter-pays” model directly to global leaders at the United Nations General Assembly, Shah stated,“Vulnerable mountain nations should receive immediate loss-and-damage compensation from the industrialized countries that fueled the crisis.” High in the Himalayas, the mud is beginning to dry, but the structural foundations of the region have changed forever. The catastrophe in northern Nepal stands as a harsh reminder that for the communities living in the shadow of the world’s highest peaks, the costs of climate change are no longer a future projection; they are already being paid in blood and stone. Why This Feels Close to Home Srinagar The air coming out of Rasuwa contains a sound I know in my bones. It is the raw, jagged panic of fractured phone calls, the sight of concrete buildings sinking into the mud like wet cardboard, and the sudden, eerie silence when the lines go silent.Watching it hit me hard in the chest. In a split second, I was pulled back to September 2014, when my own world went completely underwater during the Great Flood of Kashmir. For more than a week, the rain had been relentless. A heavy, grey sheet of water hammered our roofs, raising a collective, unspoken terror across the valley. On the day the river finally gave way, warning announcements blared through the streets hours before the breach. We took every precaution we could think of. But the truth is, no one could have anticipated the sheer scale of the devastation that downpour was carrying. “Take all your necessary documents and things to the third floor,” my father insisted. His voice was steady but urgent as he gathered the meager rations we had in store. By 3:00 AM, the noise arrived; a terrifying, low roar of gushing water. It wasn’t confined to its banks; it was tearing down our concrete roads. I ran from my room to wake the others, just as my brother came bounding downstairs, his face pale with the same fatal realization. Within minutes, the muddy, freezing water swallowed nearly two floors of every house in our community. The shock left us completely paralyzed. Suddenly, we were trapped in the desperate, narrow space between life and death. Around us, the neighborhood became a canvas of pure terror. The elderly and sick were stranded on upper levels, unable to move without help. Children shivered in the damp, biting air, crying quietly as we held them close to our chests. Pregnant mothers were terrified they would go into labor right there on the zinc roofs. My relative, Rumana, was heavily pregnant in Indranagar at the time. “The intense terror and shock brought me into labor pains which almost continued up to a week later,” she later recalled. “In the moment, I thought this is the end.” She was eventually ferried through a verandah into a rescue boat brought by a neighbor, and her daughter was born healthy a week later, against all odds. For days that bled into weeks, we lived on absolute scraps, rationing every single bite. With the cell towers drowned, our phones became useless bricks. We were entirely cut off, unable to reach neighbors just three houses away, let alone family outside the valley. That heavy, agonizing silence stretched out, leaving us completely in the dark about who was alive and who had been lost. Staring out at a vast, brown sea, it felt like the literal end of the world. Then came the agonizing choice. “We are almost out of food,” my mother whispered. We had to get the children out. When a few private boats finally paddled through the debris, our relief was instantly cut by an ugly reality: the boatmen were demanding money and gold to ferry people to safety. Even in the face of death, human greed didn’t take a back seat. My uncle pulled out a meager, crumpled sum of `3,000, pleading for our lives. The man took it. We squeezed into the boat; a mini capsule of luck floating on the lethal current. But my father refused to step in. “I am staying here,” he said flatly. “You all need to leave immediately and look for help.” Tears streamed down my face as I begged him to come, but he wouldn’t budge. In the chaos, burglaries and home invasions were rampant, and he chose to defend what little we had left. He stayed in that flooded shell of a house alone. For sixty days, while the rest of us took sanctuary in a crowded school on higher ground, my dad lived through a private, slow-motion nightmare inside our drowning home. He was entirely cut off from the world, trapped above an ocean of stagnant, toxic water and a heavy, suffocating silence. His whole universe shrank to a single, damp upper room. Food was a luxury; he survived on sheer will, meticulously rationing expired biscuits and stale rice, never knowing if the next handful would be his last. As hard as the starvation and isolation were, it was the environment that almost broke him. The floodwaters drove thousands of rodents out of the ground, and suddenly, my dad was sharing his tiny sanctuary with aggressive, displaced mice. They chewed through the last of his clean clothes, scurried over him in the pitch-black nights, and bit at his skin while he tried to sleep. The constant fear of infection, paired with that relentless, scratching sound in the dark, was pure psychological warfare. He was deeply, profoundly down, starving, mentally exhausted and quietly mourning the destruction of everything he had spent his life building. Yet, day after agonizing day, he stayed. He stood guard against the looters paddling through our old neighborhood, absolutely refusing to let the chaos steal the last remnants of our family’s dignity. When the waters finally receded after months, we were reunited. There were no celebrations, but we at least had each other. He looked at us, his voice thick with emotion, and said, “It was pure agony in there, but I just couldn’t bring myself to leave our home. I am so sorry... I tried, but I couldn’t save your childhood photographs. The water took them before I could get downstairs.” Hearing him apologize broke our hearts. He was sitting there, his body painfully thin and his hands scarred from the bites, feeling guilty about pictures. We hugged him tight and told him the truth: we didn’t care about the photos; we thanked him for saving our home, and more importantly, for surviving. Seeing his eyes through it all, unbroken despite everything, healed something deep inside us. That was the exact moment I knew, without a single doubt, that my father was the bravest man I will ever know. Coming home was its own unique trauma. The house we returned to was a rotting, mud-caked ruin, stripped of everything that made it a home. The structural integrity was completely shattered, forcing us to pull together what little strength we had left and rebuild entirely from scratch. That process broke something deep inside us. The physical exhaustion of moving damp bricks and scraping away toxic silt was nothing compared to the profound mental and emotional toll that settled over every member of my family and our community. We entered a state of collective, chronic hyper-vigilance. For years afterward, a sudden cloud-cast sky or a heavy night of rain would trigger intense panic, racing heartbeats, and sleepless nights of pacing the floor. The financial ruin strained our relationships to the breaking point, as the overwhelming weight of debt and displacement stripped away our sense of safety. Our neighbors, once vibrant and deeply connected, became isolated ghosts of themselves, navigating a quiet, unaddressed epidemic of depression and post-traumatic stress. We rebuilt the physical walls, but the invisible, psychological fractures in our well-being remained, leaving us mourning not just our lost possessions, but the secure, unburdened versions of ourselves we could never get back. The Real Cost: A Ticking Himalayan Bomb The mountains do not speak in the sterile language of policy, yet we constantly try to force them to. We split the shared trauma of the Hindu Kush-Himalaya region into tidy columns of disaster statistics, climate assessments and infrastructure budgets. But if you stand on the mud-slicked banks of the Jhelum River here in Kashmir, or walk through the shattered, terraced hillsides of Rasuwa in Nepal, the language of this crisis is visceral. It is written in the smell of river silt drying inside a ruined kitchen. It is the silence of a missing neighbor, the hollow look of a shopkeeper staring at buried inventory, and the collective terror that grips a community every time dark clouds gather on the horizon. What happened to us in Kashmir and what is unfolding in Rasuwa today are not isolated strokes of bad luck. They are the structural heartbreaks of a single, systemic failure stretching across the spine of Asia. We have misread these mountains, treating a living, shifting landscape as if it were a flat, static plain. In both Srinagar and Kathmandu, the ancient wetlands that once functioned as natural sponges, quietly absorbing the fury of heavy monsoons, have been choked under layers of concrete. Driven by an aggressive, poorly planned rush toward urbanization, we have paved over the very arteries our rivers need to flow. When the heavy rains come, the water has nowhere left to go but into our living rooms. We call this “development.” We carve massive highways into fragile, seismic slopes, erect heavy multi-story concrete buildings on loose topography, and dam pristine rivers to generate immediate revenue. We build for today’s balance sheets, completely blind to the ecological shocks of tomorrow. Meanwhile, overhead, the atmosphere is shifting. The Hindu Kush-Himalaya region is warming at a rate significantly higher than the global average. Up in the high peaks, the ice is listening. Glaciers are destabilizing, forming volatile, top-heavy glacial lakes, while predictable monsoons warp into violent, unpredictable cloudbursts. Nepal’s crisis may have begun with the roar of a high-altitude glacial collapse and Kashmir’s with the sudden sky-shattering violence of severe rainfall, but the root causes are identical, human-made, and accelerating. To halt this cycle of grief, governments across the Himalayan belt must pivot away from the exhausting cycle of reactive rescue operations. We cannot keep waiting for the tragedy to happen just so we can deploy helicopters, hand out food packets, and take photos of the devastation. We need aggressive, proactive systemic change: • Respecting the River’s Space: Enact and fiercely enforce zero-tolerance bans on commercial and residential construction within active floodplains, ancient river channels and ecological buffer zones. The rivers will always claim their paths back; it is up to us to stay out of their way. • Building for the Topography: Discard generic, flatland construction blueprints. Infrastructure in the hills must mandate climate-resilient, lightweight, and seismically flexible designs that work with the fragile topography rather than cutting aggressively into unstable slopes. • Erasing Borders for Safety: Disasters do not carry passports. We need Early Warning Systems (EWS) and integrated satellite monitoring operating seamlessly across India, Nepal, Bhutan and Pakistan. Real-time data sharing on glacial lake volumes must reach downstream communities days, not hours, before the water does. • Healing the Invisible Scars: We must acknowledge that rebuilding a life requires more than just brick, mortar, and emergency rations. Governments must integrate decentralized, trauma-informed psychological rehabilitation directly into disaster response policies. The invisible scars of displacement and loss linger for decades; our healing strategies must last just as long. The floods eventually recede, leaving behind cracked earth, ruined photographs and quiet, traumatized communities. But the systemic vulnerability remains. Until we change how we live alongside nature, we are merely waiting in line for the next inevitable tragedy. Hamna Mir, GK School of Communication alumna

My relative, Rumana, was heavily pregnant in Indranagar at the time.

stories.headline: Moody’s pegs India’s FY27 GDP growth at 7%, aided by robust consumption, investment
stories.title: Moody’s pegs India’s FY27 GDP growth at 7%, aided by robust consumption, investment
stories.summary: New Delhi, Nov 11: Moody’s Ratings on Wednesday said the Indian economy is expected to grow at 7 per cent in the current fiscal compared to 6.5 per cent pegged earlier, aided by robust consumption, improving investment dynamics and strong macroeconomic fundamentals. In its Global Macro Outlook 2027-28, Moody’s, however, said that near-term risks to growth persist as household consumption remains vulnerable to “intensifying and broadening price pressures”, with headline inflation close to the upper end of the RBI’s inflation target range, while a deficient monsoon and El Nino conditions weigh on agricultural output and rural demand. Retail inflation rose to 5.54 per cent in September 2026. “India’s broad-based economic momentum and demonstrated resilience to the energy supply shock warrant upward revisions to our 2026-27 growth forecasts to 7 per cent from 6.5 per cent,” it said. RBI estimates GDP growth of 7.1 per cent in the current fiscal, in line with OECD projection. The International Monetary Fund (IMF), ADB and S&P Global Ratings have projected a 7 per cent growth, while Fitch Ratings expects India’s GDP to grow 6.9 per cent. Moody’s said robust consumption, improving investment dynamics and strong macroeconomic fundamentals imply that the economy appears well positioned to sustain growth near 7 per cent over the medium term. A sustained private investment boom that materially boosts manufacturing, employment and productivity could lift growth rates above Moody’s baseline projections. India has adjusted to the energy price shock better than previously assumed, helped by its ability to diversify crude and gas supplies and buffer consumers from the immediate price impact through state-backed oil marketing companies and tax cuts. India is also home to the world’s largest single-site refining complex, and its large and sophisticated refining capacity has helped limit fuel supply disruptions while supporting its role as a major exporter of refined petroleum products, Moody’s added. “High frequency indicators, including robust capital goods production and imports, accelerating industrial credit growth and rising capacity utilisation, suggest that India may be at the cusp of a new private capex cycle after several years of corporate and banking- sector balance sheet repair,” the US-based agency said. Broader economic activity also remains solid amid expanding manufacturing and services purchasing manager indexes and double-digit year-on-year growth in goods and services tax revenue, vehicle sales and merchandise exports, it added. However, Moody’s said with the RBI on track to raise rates further, tighter monetary policy could delay the recovery in private investment. Moody’s said emerging markets face a more challenging external environment heading into 2027 with higher energy prices, elevated global interest rates and persistent trade and geopolitical uncertainty adding to inflation and financing pressures. At the same time, concerns over the returns on AI investment have emerged as an additional source of volatility. Quoting Institute of International Finance data, Moody’s said non-resident portfolio flows to emerging markets recorded USD 33.8 billion in outflows in October, following USD 19.3 billion in September, with the pullback concentrated in equities, particularly in Asia. “As investors become more selective, economies with strong domestic growth drivers, credible policy frameworks and solid buffers should remain relatively resilient,” Moody’s added.

stories.headline: Illegitimate, even if legal
stories.title: Illegitimate, even if legal
stories.summary: Fast on the heels of a harebrained strategy of growing its rest of India business disproportionately, J&K Bank has now come with a kowtowing recruitment policy. It doesn’t take much to see the connection between the two. Soon, to man its “growing” businesses across the country, recruitments will have to be made. The same logic that makes excessive outward lending a bad bargain for the Bank (See Debasing the J&K Bank, 3rd September 2026, Greater Kashmir) and its stakeholders applies with equal force to human capital. For now, though, for the first time in its nearly nine-decade history, the J&K Bank has applied the government’s reservation matrix to the recruitment of Probationary Officers and Banking Associates. Age limits have been tightened for open-merit candidates and relaxed for others. In a region where high-end private employment is scarce, the Bank has long been prized precisely because it selected on commercial criteria. That practice is now being rewritten. This is not a minor procedural adjustment. It marks a rupture in the institutional character of a listed commercial bank. The J&K Bank’s notifications cite the Jammu and Kashmir Reservation Rules, 2005, as amended by S.O. 176 of March 2024. But these reservations drawn from under Articles 15(4) and 16(4) are constitutional measures directed at the State and its instrumentalities. The Reserve Bank of India classifies J&K Bank as an old generation private-sector bank, even while the governments of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh hold a majority stake. The Bank also describes itself as a “scheduled commercial bank and one of the oldest private sector banks in India”. Being a “scheduled commercial bank” means J&K Bank is an ordinary, profit-oriented banking company under RBI regulation, not a government department or a public-sector undertaking in the sense used for nationalized banks. This is a key distinction. Public-sector banks such as State Bank of India and Punjab National Bank operate under the Department of Financial Services and apply DoPT reservation rules because they are nationalized entities under central ownership. J&K Bank has never been in that category. Its core activities of accepting deposits, advancing loans, and managing risk are ordinary commercial transactions of a banking company. Treating it as if it were a government department confuses ownership with constitutional status. The controlling judicial determination on this point is the 2006 Full Bench judgment of the Jammu and Kashmir High Court in Firdous Ahmad Tanki and Others v. J&K Bank Ltd. and State of J&K. After the Supreme Court set aside an earlier view, the majority held that the Bank is neither the State nor an authority or instrumentality of the State within the meaning of Article 12. An earlier Division Bench of the Jammu and Kashmir High Court in Jagdish Chander Gupta v. The Jammu and Kashmir Bank Ltd. and Ors had reached the same conclusion. It was amplified that the mere status as a “Government company” under Section 617 of the Companies Act (because the State holds a majority of the paid-up capital) is not enough to make it an instrumentality of the State. Employment decisions of the J&K Bank arise from private and contractual relations, not from sovereign obligations. It does not perform public duties or public functions while dealing with employees or carrying out normal commercial banking activities. Management rests with the Board under the Articles of Association and the Companies Act. Majority shareholding does not, by itself, create the deep and pervasive control required to treat the entity as State for fundamental-rights purposes. Even though this may not be the operational reality today. When a court has held that the Bank is not “State” and does not discharge public functions in its commercial or employment sphere, the constitutional rationale for caste- or category-based reservation does not attach. Even if a board resolution or government influence can make the policy formally possible under company law, it remains illegitimate as a matter of institutional principle. The Bank has operated since 1938 on commercial selection. Applying the full apparatus of UT reservation rules for the first time converts a profit-seeking enterprise into a vehicle for social engineering without the legal premise that the Constitution itself requires it. The analytical costs of such a conversion are straightforward. Banking rewards cognitive ability, judgment and integrity in credit appraisal, portfolio risk, compliance and customer acquisition. Rigid quotas lower effective selection thresholds for a majority of vacancies. Over successive cohorts this shifts the skill distribution within the workforce. Weaker average competence raises the probability of operational lapses and credit losses. Public-sector banks, which have long operated under reservation frameworks, have historically carried substantially higher non-performing asset ratios than private banks. For a listed or hybrid entity the costs fall on shareholders, depositors and the local economy. Minority shareholders see returns diluted when non-commercial criteria dominate hiring and promotion. Depositors face higher risk if credit judgment weakens. High-ability candidates from reserved categories often prefer pure private-sector employers that select purely on merit; open-merit candidates face reduced opportunities and lower expected returns to effort. What begins as a recruitment policy becomes a gradual alteration of the Bank’s DNA from a commercial intermediary that mobilizes local savings and deploys them productively to a quasi-administrative organization responsive to political and social pressures. Alternatives exist that address historical disadvantages without permanently lowering selection standards in commercial roles. The most effective long-term approach is input-focused: expanding free or heavily subsidized coaching, scholarships, skill programs and preparatory courses targeted at disadvantaged groups so that more candidates clear open-merit thresholds. This raises both equity and the absolute quality of the talent pool. Voluntary affirmative action offers another path. Outreach, targeted internships, apprenticeships and diversity goals can operate without relaxing the final selection standard. Blind hiring techniques and stronger anti-discrimination enforcement address residual bias. Any preference mechanism should include sunset clauses and periodic review against capability metrics, with automatic phase-down once educational and representation gaps narrow. These approaches locate the remedy primarily in education and opportunity rather than permanent outcome quotas. In a commercial enterprise the distinction is decisive: one raises absolute competence; the other systematically lowers standards. J&K Bank’s history, RBI classification and judicial status establish that it is not required to function as a public-sector undertaking for reservation purposes. The first-time application of a 60 per-cent matrix is therefore not fulfilment of a constitutional obligation but a choice that trades commercial efficiency for other objectives. That choice may be formally sustainable. It is not legitimate if the goal is to preserve an institution capable of intermediating local savings into productive credit on a sustainable basis. The Bank’s shareholders, depositors and the regional economy have a direct interest in keeping selection criteria aligned with the commercial functions the institution was created to perform. Postscript There has been a widespread political reaction to the Bank’s recruitment notification. The irony in this political hypocrisy is hard to miss. Regional parties rightly call the reservation matrix an assault on merit and an act of exclusion. In the same breath, they demand the upper age limit be raised from 30 to 40 years. Reserved-category candidates already enjoy generous age relaxations. Stretching the ceiling to 40 simply swells their pool further, while open-merit candidates get little more than a polite nod. This is not a defence of competence. It is a negotiation for a larger share inside the very framework they pretend to oppose. They cry foul over reservations, then lobby for the relaxations that entrench them, all while striking the pose of protectors of merit. It is the familiar tragedy of the political class: ignorance dressed up as messianism. Better to have clear-eyed adversaries who understand the institution than these self-appointed saviours who endanger it in the name of saving it. The author is a Contributing Editor of Greater Kashmir.

stories.headline: Cabinet clears Rs 3,230-crore Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum at North, South Blocks
stories.title: Cabinet clears Rs 3,230-crore Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum at North, South Blocks
stories.summary: New Delhi, Nov 11: The Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs, chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, on Wednesday approved the development of the Yuge Yugeen Bharat Museum at the historic North and South Block complex in New Delhi at an estimated cost of Rs 3,230 crore. Envisaged as a landmark civilizational museum showcasing India’s rich and diverse heritage, the project will transform the historical government buildings into a major public cultural institution while preserving their architectural character. With a proposed built-up area of around 1,78,509 square metres, the museum is expected to have the world’s largest display area. The project will be implemented in phases between 2026-27 and 2030-31. The first gallery, based on the theme of ‘Adornment’, is expected to open to the public in the North Block in the latter part of 2027. According to the government, around 1.8 million objects have been identified from the National Museum and other museums under the Ministry of Culture, 52 Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) site museums, state museums and private collections for display at the proposed museum. Other galleries will cover themes such as architecture and cityscapes, mathematics and astronomy, languages and scripts, faith and spirituality, and India’s historical connections with the world through trade and ideas. The museum will combine traditional exhibitions with modern museum practices, immersive technologies and visitor-friendly facilities. It will also have collection storage and conservation facilities, landscaping, intelligent building systems and other associated infrastructure. The museum project was announced by the Prime Minister on May 18, 2023. Following the relocation of government offices from the North and South Blocks, the buildings are being repurposed for cultural and public use. The government said the museum would serve as a major destination for domestic and international tourists while providing opportunities for education, research and engagement with India’s civilizational heritage. It is being designed to accommodate around one crore visitors annually. The project is also expected to generate employment for artisans, craftspeople, researchers, museologists, designers, performers and other professionals, besides supporting tourism and hospitality-related livelihoods. It will promote domestic manufacturing of museum materials and products under the Make in India initiative. The museum is expected to generate revenue through ticket sales, food and beverage facilities, events, venue rentals, guided tours, digital experiences and retail outlets. The proposal was appraised by the Public Investment Board on July 27, 2026, and the Ministry of Culture has concurred with its recommendations.

stories.headline: Kashmir Wazas to enforce 10 pm Wazwan curfew
stories.title: Kashmir Wazas to enforce 10 pm Wazwan curfew
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 11: Kashmir’s traditional Wazas have decided not to serve Wazwan at weddings and other functions beyond 10 pm, drawing a firm line against what they describe as increasingly late-night wedding schedules and the inhuman working conditions faced by chefs and their assistants. The decision was taken unanimously at a meeting of the Kashmir Waza Association held at a marriage hall in the Rajouri Kadal area of Srinagar on Wednesday. Members said Wazas and their workers were routinely made to work for unusually long hours, sometimes continuing until after Fajr prayers, without adequate arrangements for rest. Association president Ghulam Nabi Baba said the Waza community had suffered in silence for a long time, even as late-night wedding functions had become increasingly common. “Such is the situation we have reached. We are being treated inhumanely. Our workers report for work at 10 am and are made to work until the following morning, sometimes even after Fajr prayers. Nobody seems concerned about their condition,” Baba said. He explained that preparing Wazwan itself involved several hours of work, followed by lengthy serving schedules. Waza teams are generally expected to serve lunch from around 1 pm to 6 pm, after which they have to prepare for dinner service, which often begins well into the night. The situation becomes particularly difficult when Wazas are engaged at the bride’s residence, where they are required to wait for the groom and his entourage to arrive before the wedding proceedings can be completed. Baba recalled an incident in which a groom arrived at around 1:30 am, by which time the Maulvi invited to solemnise the Nikah had already left after waiting for him. The family subsequently approached a local Imam, who initially expressed his inability to perform the Nikah, saying he did not have the necessary expertise, but was eventually persuaded to solemnise the marriage. “There have been incidents where the Maulvi left without solemnising the Nikah because the groom did not turn up till 1 am. We are also humans. So we have now set the 10 pm deadline,” Baba said. He said arriving late for wedding feasts had become a fashion and appealed to people to abandon the practice, pointing out that the Wazwan involved several categories of workers whose working hours and dignity also needed to be respected. “Going late to wedding feasts has become fashionable. People need to get rid of this bad habit. There are so many people attached to the Wazwan, and they too have the right to dignified working hours,” he said. Apart from prolonged working hours, the association raised concerns over the facilities provided to Wazas and their workers at wedding venues. Members alleged that workers were often not provided proper arrangements for rest, with some being made to sleep on torn or foul-smelling bedding despite families spending lakhs of rupees on other wedding arrangements. They questioned why basic facilities were overlooked for the very people responsible for preparing and serving one of the most important elements of Kashmiri wedding celebrations. “People spend lakhs of rupees on different wedding arrangements, but when it comes to providing us with basic facilities, even clean bedding is not ensured. We are sometimes given torn or smelly bedding. Is this how people should be treated?” members asked. One of the chefs said workers needed a proper place to sleep and recover after spending long hours preparing and serving food, particularly when they were expected to resume their duties the following day. “We work long hours and need some time to rest before we prepare ourselves for the next day’s gruelling routine. The hosts should take care of that aspect,” he said. The association said the contribution of Wazas and their workers to Kashmir’s traditional wedding culture should be accompanied by respect for their working conditions. Members maintained that the profession could not be expected to function on schedules that left workers exhausted and deprived them of adequate rest. Reiterating the decision, Baba said the association had unanimously resolved that no Waza in Kashmir would serve at weddings or other functions beyond 10 pm. The decision, he said, was intended to ensure that workers were not kept engaged throughout the night and could leave after their scheduled working hours. The association said the decision would apply collectively to Waza service providers across Kashmir and appealed to families to organise wedding functions in a manner that allowed the food service to conclude by the stipulated time.

Nobody seems concerned about their condition,” Baba said.
He explained that preparing Wazwan itself involved several hours of work, followed by lengthy serving schedules.

The situation becomes particularly difficult when Wazas are engaged at the bride’s residence, where they are required to wait for the groom and his entourage to arrive before the wedding proceedings can be completed.
Baba recalled an incident in which a groom arrived at around 1:30 am, by which time the Maulvi invited to solemnise the Nikah had already left after waiting for him.

The family subsequently approached a local Imam, who initially expressed his inability to perform the Nikah, saying he did not have the necessary expertise, but was eventually persuaded to solemnise the marriage.
“There have been incidents where the Maulvi left without solemnising the Nikah because the groom did not turn up till 1 am.
We are also humans.
So we have now set the 10 pm deadline,” Baba said.

He said arriving late for wedding feasts had become a fashion and appealed to people to abandon the practice, pointing out that the Wazwan involved several categories of workers whose working hours and dignity also needed to be respected.
“Going late to wedding feasts has become fashionable.
People need to get rid of this bad habit.
There are so many people attached to the Wazwan, and they too have the right to dignified working hours,” he said.
Apart from prolonged working hours, the association raised concerns over the facilities provided to Wazas and their workers at wedding venues.

Members alleged that workers were often not provided proper arrangements for rest, with some being made to sleep on torn or foul-smelling bedding despite families spending lakhs of rupees on other wedding arrangements.
They questioned why basic facilities were overlooked for the very people responsible for preparing and serving one of the most important elements of Kashmiri wedding celebrations.
“People spend lakhs of rupees on different wedding arrangements, but when it comes to providing us with basic facilities, even clean bedding is not ensured.
We are sometimes given torn or smelly bedding.
Is this how people should be treated?” members asked.

One of the chefs said workers needed a proper place to sleep and recover after spending long hours preparing and serving food, particularly when they were expected to resume their duties the following day.
“We work long hours and need some time to rest before we prepare ourselves for the next day’s gruelling routine.
The hosts should take care of that aspect,” he said.
The association said the contribution of Wazas and their workers to Kashmir’s traditional wedding culture should be accompanied by respect for their working conditions.
Members maintained that the profession could not be expected to function on schedules that left workers exhausted and deprived them of adequate rest.
Reiterating the decision, Baba said the association had unanimously resolved that no Waza in Kashmir would serve at weddings or other functions beyond 10 pm.
The decision, he said, was intended to ensure that workers were not kept engaged throughout the night and could leave after their scheduled working hours.

The association said the decision would apply collectively to Waza service providers across Kashmir and appealed to families to organise wedding functions in a manner that allowed the food service to conclude by the stipulated time.

stories.headline: Light snow in Kashmir heights, Mughal Road shut ahead of fresh spell
stories.title: Light snow in Kashmir heights, Mughal Road shut ahead of fresh spell
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 11: Higher reaches of Kashmir received fresh snowfall on Wednesday under the influence of a feeble Western Disturbance, while a stronger system is expected to bring widespread rain to the plains and moderate to heavy snowfall in higher reaches of Jammu and Kashmir from November 12 to 14. The fresh precipitation prompted authorities to close the Mughal Road ahead of the forecast spell after snowfall and rain made the Peer Ki Gali stretch slippery. Gurez and Tulail valleys in north Kashmir also received fresh snowfall. Officials said the Mughal Road, which connects south Kashmir with Rajouri and Poonch districts, was closed as a precautionary measure. Commuters have been advised to avoid the route until further clearance. Director Meteorological Centre Srinagar, Dr Mukhtar Ahmad, said the ongoing feeble Western Disturbance was causing light precipitation over isolated higher reaches, while a relatively stronger system would trigger the main weather activity from the early hours of November 12. “This is a significant weather system. While rainfall will dominate in the plains, we expect light to moderate snowfall across tourist places, marking the season’s first snowfall in Doodhpathri, Pahalgam, Gulmarg and Sonamarg,” Ahmad said. He said higher reaches and mountain passes, including Peer Ki Gali, Sinthan Top, Margan Top, Zojila, Razdan Pass and Sadhna Top, were likely to receive moderate to heavy snowfall, with accumulations of one to two feet possible at some locations. The Meteorological Centre has also indicated a 50 percent possibility of light snowfall or mixed precipitation over the plains of Shopian, Kulgam, Kupwara, Bandipora and adjoining areas. The main spell is expected to intensify on November 12 and continue until the morning of November 14. While widespread rainfall is likely in the plains, middle reaches may receive light snowfall and higher reaches moderate to heavy snowfall. The upper reaches of Chenab Valley, including Kishtwar, Doda and Ramban, and the PirPanjal range in Rajouri and Poonch districts are also likely to receive snow. The weather system could disrupt traffic on several important mountain routes, including the Srinagar-Leh highway via Zojila, Mughal Road, Sinthan Top, Margan Top, Razdan Top and Sadhna Pass. These routes connect Kashmir with Ladakh, Rajouri-Poonch, Kishtwar, the Warwan-Marwah valleys, Gurez-Tulail and Karnah. Snow accumulation and reduced visibility could temporarily affect movement, particularly at higher elevations. In view of the forecast, the Bandipora district administration has temporarily prohibited tourists from visiting Gurez and Tulail Valley and asked those already staying there to plan their departure immediately in coordination with the District Control Room. Candidates scheduled to appear in the Accounts Assistant written examination on November 15 have been advised to plan their journeys in advance and reach their examination centres before weather conditions deteriorate. The administration has also advised expectant mothers living in upper reaches, whose expected dates of delivery fall within the next month, to shift to nearby hospitals to ensure timely medical assistance in case snowfall disrupts road connectivity. Residents have been urged to avoid unnecessary travel to Gurez and other higher reaches and refrain from organising social gatherings in vulnerable areas during the forecast period. Meanwhile, the Anantnag district administration has activated its District Emergency Operation Centre round the clock to deal with weather-related emergencies and public grievances. Departments, including Public Works (R&B), Mechanical Engineering, Revenue, Flood Control, PMGSY, Urban Local Bodies, KPDCL, Jal Shakti and Health and Medical Education, have been directed to take precautionary measures and keep manpower and machinery ready. The administration has issued helpline numbers 01932-227112, 9697982527, 7780885759 and 9419091681 for public assistance. Farmers have also been advised to suspend harvesting operations on November 12 and 13 and ensure that harvested crops are safely stored to prevent damage from rain and snowfall.
